localBiteReport: Note: The most current sourced reports are from late July to early August 2026, roughly one to two weeks old. Speckled trout and redfish are the headline inshore species on Choctawhatchee Bay right now, with local guides reporting solid trout action across the bay and at least one angler landing a 40-inch, 26-pound bull redfish out of Santa Rosa Beach. Black drum and flounder are also showing up as bay targets for August. Water temperature is 86°F, and the summer heat is pushing guides to strongly recommend early morning trips — topwater action can be explosive at first light before the sun gets high, with docks, grass flats, oyster beds, and bridge structure all holding fish as the day warms. Live bait (shrimp, pinfish, finger mullet) is the top producer, though soft plastics and shallow-running plugs are working for reds around bridge pilings and passes on outgoing tides.

aiSummary: Choctawhatchee Bay is fishing well this Saturday, with speckled trout and redfish leading a solid inshore bite across the bay — guides have been reporting consistent trout action and at least one big bull redfish in the mix recently. Get on the water early: the heat index will push past 100°F by midday, and a 23% chance of afternoon thunderstorms opens up after 1 PM, making a morning departure strongly advisable. Light east winds of 0–5 mph mean flat, calm conditions at first light, and a waning crescent moon is delivering a strong tidal push — time your moves around the falling tide toward the 1:42 PM low for the best midday bite before weather threatens.

bridge.aiNote: The 331 Bridge spans a narrow neck of Choctawhatchee Bay, creating a natural current funnel that pushes bait through on both tides — pilings hold speckled trout, redfish, sheepshead, and black drum year-round. The lee-side pilings are the prime ambush zone, especially on an incoming tide, as predators stack up waiting for bait swept through the funnel. Because the open water here is fully exposed to wind and chop, it's typically the first spot on the bay to become unfishable when conditions deteriorate.
bridge.todaysCall: Today's light east wind of 0–5 mph is ideal for the bridge — minimal chop and no wave interference with your presentations around the pilings. Work the lee-side structure early at first light; the falling tide toward the 1:42 PM low will create the strongest current push through the funnel, concentrating bait and the fish that follow. Soft plastics and live shrimp worked tight to the pilings are the call, with black drum and sheepshead likely holding in the deeper scour zones below the structure. Be off the open water well before 1 PM given the afternoon storm window — the bridge offers no shelter if a cell rolls through.

alaqua.aiNote: Alaqua Bayou is a protected, sheltered fishery with a strong year-round redfish population, plus trout and flounder at the mouth. The oyster bars at the creek mouth are the prime target zone, and tree cover keeps water temperatures a few degrees cooler than the open bay while also providing a buffer from wind and weather. The upper creek transitions toward brackish water, where bass begin to mix with smaller redfish.
alaqua.todaysCall: The tree-lined, protected character of Alaqua Bayou makes it a smart choice on a hot August morning — that shade buffer matters when surface temps hit 86°F and the air feels like 102°F. Start at the oyster bars at the creek mouth right at sunrise around 6:06 AM; guides have been reporting strong trout action on grass and structure early, and live shrimp or soft plastics worked over the bar edges should be productive. The falling tide toward the 1:42 PM low will drain the bayou's shallows and concentrate redfish near the mouth and deeper creek bends — a great mid-morning move. With storms possible after 1 PM, the sheltered interior of Alaqua gives you a safe place to keep fishing if you want to push the morning window.

basin.aiNote: Basin Bayou sees noticeably less fishing pressure than Alaqua or LaGrange, which means the redfish, trout, and occasional pompano here tend to be less educated and more willing to eat. Interior grass flats offer classic sight-fishing opportunities for redfish in under two feet of water, and pompano occasionally show at the bayou mouth on moving tides in late spring and early summer. Basin is less protected than LaGrange when weather builds, so it's better suited to calm or light-wind days.
basin.todaysCall: With east winds at 0–5 mph today, Basin Bayou's relative lack of wind protection is a non-issue — it's about as fishable as it ever gets. Hit the interior grass flats at first light for sight-fishing reds in the skinny water; the strong tidal push from the waning crescent spring tide will give the shallows good water movement to activate fish. Work the bayou mouth on the falling tide toward early afternoon when bait concentrates on the drop, and keep an eye on the clock — with afternoon storms possible after 1 PM and Basin offering less cover than some alternatives, plan to wrap up and head in by midday. Live shrimp and natural-colored soft plastics are the safest bets in the slightly stained water conditions today.

lagrange.aiNote: LaGrange Bayou is regarded as the top trout producer in this part of Choctawhatchee Bay, with legendary oyster bars at the mouth and interior grass flats that hold redfish year-round. Deep holes inside the bayou hold black drum and sheepshead, giving it a diverse target list beyond the headliner species. It's also the most protected water on this side of the bay, making it the go-to destination when weather threatens.
lagrange.todaysCall: LaGrange is arguably the strongest call on the dashboard today — the legendary oyster bars at the mouth are primed for early morning topwater and live-shrimp action, and recent reports confirm guides are stacking trout across the bay right now, making LaGrange's premier trout habitat a natural focal point. Fish the mouth structure hard from sunrise through the falling tide; the strong spring-tide current will sweep bait across those oyster bars and trigger aggressive feeding. Slightly stained water today works in your favor — it gives redfish and trout more confidence in shallow ambush positions along the bar edges. With storms possible after 1 PM and LaGrange being the bay's most protected fishery, you can comfortably fish later into the morning here than almost anywhere else on this list.

fourmile.aiNote: Four Mile Creek is a tidal creek running between Shipyard Marina and the bay, where incoming tides push baitfish up into the bends and grass edges, concentrating redfish and trout. The creek mouth is a reliable flounder zone, and the upper section transitions to brackish water where bass mix with smaller reds. Short and well-protected, it's widely considered the safest fishery on this part of the bay when weather threatens.
fourmile.todaysCall: Four Mile Creek's protected nature and short layout make it a low-risk, high-reward option for a hot Saturday with afternoon storms on the forecast. Fish the creek mouth for flounder and trout early, then follow the falling tide back into the bends and grass edges as water drains the shallows and concentrates redfish through the mid-morning hours. Live shrimp tipped on a light jig head is a strong all-around choice in the slightly stained water, covering flounder near the bottom and trout in the mid-column simultaneously. If afternoon storms materialize earlier than expected, Four Mile Creek's enclosed layout is your safest retreat on this side of the bay.

hogtown.aiNote: Hogtown Bayou is one of the most productive trout flats on Choctawhatchee Bay and a signature Santa Rosa Beach guide destination, with trout reliably stacked on grass in two to four feet of water during summer mornings. Spanish mackerel show at the bayou mouth on moving tides, adding a bonus target to the mix. It sits further from the 331 Bridge than the other bayous on this dashboard, so factor in the additional run time when planning your morning.
hogtown.todaysCall: Hogtown is built for exactly this kind of morning — dead calm east winds and a strong tidal push make the grass flats ideal for early topwater and soft-plastic presentations on stacked summer trout. Guides have been hammering trout across the bay on first-light sessions, and Hogtown's reputation as the bay's signature trout flat puts it at the top of the list if you're chasing that species specifically today. Spanish mackerel may show at the mouth as the falling tide builds current heading toward the 1:42 PM low — have a faster retrieve and a spoon or swim shad ready to capitalize. Account for the longer run time when planning your departure; with storms possible after 1 PM, you'll want to be back at the ramp or in protected water well before that window opens.

mallet.aiNote: Mallet Bayou is a small tributary feeding directly into LaGrange Bayou, the bay's top trout producer, just south of Freeport. Its direct connection to LaGrange means the oyster-bar trout-and-redfish pattern associated with that larger system plausibly extends into this quieter, smaller water. It's an interior spot with limited documented fishing history, but its size and position make it a natural calm-water fallback when wind picks up on the open bay.
mallet.todaysCall: Today's near-calm winds make Mallet worth exploring as an extension of a LaGrange Bayou outing — fish LaGrange's mouth and oyster bars first, then work up into Mallet on the falling tide as fish move with the current into the smaller tributary's bends and edges. Redfish and trout are the plausible targets given the LaGrange connection, and slightly stained water should help you sneak into tighter spaces without spooking fish in the skinny interior sections. Keep expectations measured — documented action here is limited — but the quiet water and lower pressure could surprise you. Given the afternoon storm window, Mallet's protected interior is a comfortable place to extend the morning session past when you'd want to be on open water.

mack.aiNote: Mack Bayou sits on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, well west of the 331 Bridge — it's a long-run destination that's best planned as a dedicated trip rather than a quick stop. It shares the protected-bayou character of spots like Alaqua and LaGrange, with marsh grass, oyster bars, and interior holes, and it sees less pressure simply because of its distance from the main boat ramps. Hewett Bayou and Buck Bayou sit immediately to the east and are realistically fishable in the same outing.
mack.todaysCall: The long run to Mack Bayou is most justified on a calm day — and today's 0–5 mph east winds are about as flat as you'll get in August, making the crossing manageable. Pair the trip with Hewett and Buck Bayou immediately to the east to make the run worthwhile; target the oyster bars and marsh grass edges early for redfish and trout, then work interior holes for flounder as the falling tide progresses toward the 1:42 PM low. Light pressure here means less-educated fish, which can translate to more aggressive bites on live shrimp and soft plastics in the slightly stained water. Commit to an early start and a firm turnaround time — the distance back to the ramp plus a post-1 PM storm window means you cannot afford to linger on this one.

hewett.aiNote: Hewett Bayou sits immediately east of Mack Bayou on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay, near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park — another long-run spot that pairs naturally with Mack and Buck Bayou as part of a dedicated 30-A side trip. The habitat mirrors its neighbors: oyster bars and marsh grass at the mouth with deeper interior holes further in. Light pressure from its distance means fish here tend to see fewer lures and baits than on the more accessible north-shore bayous.
hewett.todaysCall: Like Mack Bayou next door, Hewett is most worth the long run on a calm-wind day — and today's near-flat east winds give you the green light if you're committed to the 30-A side of the bay. Fish the oyster bar mouth structure at first light for trout and reds, then probe the deeper interior holes for flounder as the falling tide develops through the morning. Slightly stained water calls for natural-colored soft plastics or live shrimp rather than flashy artificials, keeping presentations believable in reduced visibility. Build in plenty of buffer time: the run back across the bay with a 1 PM storm window is not a situation where you want to be cutting it close.

buck.aiNote: Buck Bayou is the smallest and least-documented of the three neighboring bayous on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park. Its habitat should track its larger neighbors — marsh grass, some oyster structure, and a modest interior — but there's less basis to speak with confidence about it as a standalone fishery. It's best treated as a bonus stop on a Mack and Hewett Bayou trip rather than a primary destination in its own right.
buck.todaysCall: Buck Bayou makes the most sense today as a quick bonus stop after fishing Mack and Hewett — don't build a dedicated run around it, but if you're already on that side of the bay it's worth a look. Work any visible oyster structure at the mouth and grass edges for redfish and trout early, keeping presentations natural-colored and near the bottom given the slightly stained water. Because this is the smallest and most speculative of the three neighboring bayous, spend 20–30 minutes here at most before moving on to better-documented water. The afternoon storm window applies with full force on this long-run side of the bay — be heading back well before 1 PM regardless of how the bite feels.
